lines: I.  Introduction

A class contains a safe tips and b unsafe tips in a finite set T. A world is the unsafe set W ⊆ T with |W| = b. Observations reveal only unsafe tips, so a transcript is a revealed subset R ⊆ W. The task is to name a safe tip, not to identify W.

That distinction is the point. Identifying the world is a coupon-collector problem whose cost grows with the number of classes; naming a safe tip need not be. The question is how much cheaper deciding is than recovering, and whether the natural decoder — name a tip drawn uniformly from the unexplored set — is actually optimal or merely convenient.
II.  Methodology

Every statement displayed below is machine-checked, with no unproved step anywhere in the chain.  STEP 1 — THE SAMPLING LAW  (C5). HOW IT IS CLOSED. The per-draw avoidance probability is computed by a product over the finite index set; the expectation of the product of unseen indicators is obtained by exchanging two finite sums, which is exact and needs no independence assumption between classes. STEP 2 — THE DECODER AND ITS RISK  (C1). WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 1. Step 1 gives what a transcript reveals; Step 2 asks what a decoder can do with it. The key counting fact is that every world compatible with a transcript has exactly b unsafe tips and contains all revealed ones, so the number still hidden is the same in all of them:

III.  Results

DECIDING IS FLAT IN K; RECOVERING IS NOT. Across the parameter grid the exact decide count is independent of the number of classes while the exact recovery count grows, and the ratio between them grows without bound as K increases. Both counts are exact integers computed from the closed forms, not simulated.

THE DECODER IS OPTIMAL, NOT MERELY FLAT. With Step 5 the equivariant decoder is a least element of the achievable worst-case risks, so no decision rule whatsoever — randomised or not, adaptive or not — achieves a smaller worst case on this problem.

Fig. 2.  The recovery identity against the process it describes. The line is equality, not a fit; the classes interact, so agreement checks the identity itself.
IV.  Discussion

THE SEPARATION OVER THE WHOLE GRID, NOT TWELVE CELLS. 1080 cells reaching 1024 classes. At P = 1/2 and ε = 1/100, recovery costs the same 6 samples as deciding at one class, 17 at two, and 22,192 at 1024 — a factor of 3699. The separation is not an overhead a larger budget absorbs; it widens without bound. THE GROWTH HAS A SHAPE. Fitting N_rec ≈ c·(K/P)(ln K + ln 1/ε) over each of 54 (P, ε) slices gives c between 0.916 and 0.966 with R² at least 0.99996 — the coupon-collector scale quoted for orientation is the right one, with a constant just under one. THE IDENTITY AGAINST THE PROCESS IT DESCRIBES. Equation (6) is an inclusion–exclusion over events that are NOT independent — the classes compete for the same N observations — and it is derived rather than measured. Simulating the process and comparing: over 200 cells the measured value differs from the identity by at most 0.0043 and 2.98 standard errors, which over that many cells is what the null predicts. ONE THING NOT TO MISREAD. The flatness of the decide cost in K is STRUCTURAL: K does not appear in the formula. The flat lines restate the theorem; what is measured is the growth beside them.
Fig. 3.  The obstruction pairwise reasoning cannot see. Every pair of worlds admits a safe coordinate; no coordinate works for all three.
V.  Conclusions

Deciding and identifying are different problems, and the gap between them is not an overhead a larger budget absorbs. The decoder is minimax over ALL decision rules, not merely flat; the decide cost is exactly ½(1−P)^N and contains no K; and recovery grows on a coupon-collector scale with a constant just under one, reaching 3699 times the decide cost at 1024 classes. The recovery identity assumes nothing about how classes interact, and simulating the process they actually follow reproduces it in every cell tested.
How the numbers were produced

PRECISION IS SET FROM THE PROBLEM, NOT PICKED. The recovery sum alternates with binomial weights and loses about K bits to cancellation — at K = 128 the largest term already exceeds the answer by eighteen orders of magnitude. Working precision is therefore 120 + ⌈K·log₁₀ 2⌉ + 40 digits, 469 at K = 1024. A fixed precision would return noise at the top of the grid. THREE SELF-CHECKS RUN BEFORE ANY RESULT IS REPORTED. The recovery risk at K = 1 must equal the decide risk exactly in rational arithmetic — the one point where the two sides must agree. The high-precision and exact-rational evaluations must agree. And the sandwich ½·Pr(U>0) ≤ R_rec ≤ Pr(U>0) must hold. All three do. THRESHOLDS ARE INVERTED BY BISECTION over exact evaluations, so the integers are true thresholds rather than rounded logarithms.
